## Why b6 was better than c8

**c8 flipped 6 discs but they were mostly edge/corner-adjacent squares** — exactly the discs White can flip back easily. c8 is an edge move, and its sandwich directions (c7, d8, b7, etc.) all run along the bottom row — a line White can attack.

**b6 flipped fewer discs but they were interior** (b5, a5, c5, c6) — much harder for White to reverse. b6 is a structurally central move.

The principle: **scoring moves vs. structural moves.** In endgame, durable interior discs matter more than many flippable edge discs. c8's 6 flips looked great on turn 1, but White spent the rest of the game chipping away at that line.

**c8 also didn't address the empty a8 corner.** It let White keep planning around a8 the whole game.

## Why a7 backfired

a7 is the C-square to a8. After Black plays a7, the corner a8 becomes sandwichable for White: a8(W) — a7(B) — a6(W). White takes the corner with a8, then the entire a-file, b-file, and c-file cascade to White (exactly what the final board shows).

## Why g2 backfired

g2 flipped 1 disc (f2) far from a8. It was a "free" move that **didn't contest the corner**. By playing g2, Black effectively skipped a turn in the a8 battle. Meanwhile White kept maneuvering until a8 was theirs.

**The lesson:** when an empty corner exists, every move should either (1) secure that corner, (2) prevent opponent from securing it, or (3) flip durable interior discs. b6 did #3. c8 sort of did #3 (but edge-flips aren't durable). a7 failed #2. g2 did neither.
